Predicting recurrence-free survival in the GBSG cohort¶

BIOF3001 — model comparison using the 13-step workflow

I compare survival random forest, XGBoost AFT and linear survival SVM against a Cox proportional-hazards baseline. I use package implementations and short wrappers to connect their different APIs; I do not implement the algorithms from scratch. The supplied file is data/gbsg.csv (the requested gbsv.csv appears to be a typo).

To run: install requirements_survival.txt with Python 3.12 and select that environment as the notebook kernel. The saved notebook includes executed results.

Step 1 — Define the aim¶

My aim is to estimate recurrence-free survival for women with node-positive breast cancer after treatment assignment. The intended use is an educational comparison of prognosis and hypothetical follow-up decisions; no clinicians were consulted. I use a three-year assessment horizon and the same eight predictors for all models. I select a probability model using nested-validation Brier scores, before looking at the holdout results. The imports below use published package implementations.

In [1]:

Step 2 — Develop new models¶

These are new fits on GBSG, not updates of the published fitted models. The papers guide my algorithm choices, but GBSG has different variables and a smaller cohort.

Reference Method used here
Chen et al. (2026) XGBoost AFT and survival SVM
Völkel et al. (2021), INFLUENCE 2.0 Survival random forest
Van Maaren et al. (2025), INFLUENCE 3.0 Survival forests and internal validation

The baseline is a Cox PH model with a small ridge-penalty grid. I do not transfer unavailable author weights or claim to reproduce their reported performance. The existing gbsg_exploratory.ipynb contains the earlier Cox diagnostic analysis; proportional-hazards and functional-form limitations still apply to this baseline.

Step 3 — Define the outcome¶

According to the GBSG data dictionary, rfstime is days to recurrence, death or last follow-up. status=1 means recurrence or death; status=0 means right censoring. I keep time and status together rather than turn the data into recurrence/no-recurrence classes.

Step 4 — Choose candidate predictors¶

I retain age, menopausal status, tumour size, grade, positive nodes, ER, progesterone receptor and assigned hormonal therapy. ER and progesterone receptor are the two biomarkers. IDs and outcomes are not predictors. Continuous values stay continuous; grade is categorical. HER2, Ki-67 and P53 are not available in this file.

Step 6 — Consider sample size and split the data¶

I reserve 20% of patients as a holdout, stratified by event status. All tuning and model selection use the other 80%. The cohort has 686 patients, below the review's 1,000-patient paper criterion. Events per Cox coefficient are descriptive, not a formal sample-size calculation or proof that the ML models are adequately powered.

In [5]:

Step 7 — Handle missing predictors¶

This file has no missing values; its source already retained complete cases from the original trial. I still put median/mode imputation inside each training pipeline for future missing predictors. Scaling and encoding are also learned within folds. Nodes and receptors use log1p to reduce skew while retaining zeros.

In [6]:
preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ('numeric', make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy='median'), StandardScaler()), numeric),
    ('log', make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy='median'),
                          FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out='one-to-one'),
                          StandardScaler()), log_numeric),
    ('category', make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent'),
                               OneHotEncoder(drop='first', handle_unknown='ignore',
                                             sparse_output=False)), categorical)
], verbose_feature_names_out=False)

Step 8 — Fit the prediction models¶

I use small, prespecified grids with three-fold inner validation. Cox and SVM use regularisation; the forest has shallow trees and minimum leaf sizes. No univariate screening is used. The XGBoost part adapts the official AFT example: an event has bounds [time, time] and a censored observation [time, infinity]. The wrapper only joins package fitting and validation calls.

In [7]:
configs = {
    'Cox': (CoxPHSurvivalAnalysis(ties='efron'), {'model__alpha': [0.01, 1, 10]}),
    'RForest': (RandomSurvivalForest(n_estimators=200, max_depth=5, max_features=0.7,
                                     n_jobs=1, random_state=SEED),
                {'model__min_samples_leaf': [10, 20]}),
    'SVM': (FastSurvivalSVM(rank_ratio=1, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-6, random_state=SEED),
            {'model__alpha': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1]})
}
AFT_SCALE = 1.0
aft_params = dict(objective='survival:aft', eval_metric='aft-nloglik', tree_method='hist',
                  aft_loss_distribution='normal', aft_loss_distribution_scale=AFT_SCALE,
                  learning_rate=0.05, reg_lambda=10, min_child_weight=5, seed=SEED, nthread=1)
aft_grid = list(ParameterGrid({'max_depth': [1, 2]}))
names, probability_names = ['Cox', 'RForest', 'XGBoost', 'SVM'], ['Cox', 'RForest', 'XGBoost']

def fit_model(name, x, target):
    folds = list(StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED).split(x, target['status']))
    if name != 'XGBoost':
        estimator, grid = configs[name]
        pipeline = Pipeline([('pre', clone(preprocess)), ('model', clone(estimator))])
        search = GridSearchCV(pipeline, grid, cv=folds, n_jobs=1, error_score='raise')
        search.fit(x, target)  # Survival estimators score with Harrell's C-index.
        return search.best_estimator_, search.best_params_
    scores = []
    for candidate in aft_grid:
        fold_scores = []
        for tr, va in folds:
            pre = clone(preprocess)
            z = pre.fit_transform(x.iloc[tr])
            train = xgb.DMatrix(z, label_lower_bound=target['rfstime'][tr],
                                label_upper_bound=np.where(target['status'][tr], target['rfstime'][tr], np.inf))
            booster = xgb.train(aft_params | candidate, train, num_boost_round=150)
            risk = -booster.predict(xgb.DMatrix(pre.transform(x.iloc[va])), output_margin=True)
            fold_scores.append(concordance_index_censored(target['status'][va], target['rfstime'][va], risk)[0])
        scores.append(np.mean(fold_scores))
    best = aft_grid[int(np.argmax(scores))]
    pre = clone(preprocess)
    train = xgb.DMatrix(pre.fit_transform(x), label_lower_bound=target['rfstime'],
                        label_upper_bound=np.where(target['status'], target['rfstime'], np.inf))
    return (pre, xgb.train(aft_params | best, train, num_boost_round=150)), best

The next wrapper obtains predictions from the fitted packages. For normal-error AFT, SciPy converts the predicted log-time into survival probabilities using the specified AFT distribution. SVM supplies a risk ranking only; I do not turn its scores into invented probabilities or add a second calibration model.

In [8]:
def predict_model(name, model, x):
    if name == 'XGBoost':
        pre, booster = model
        mu = booster.predict(xgb.DMatrix(pre.transform(x)), output_margin=True)
        return -mu, norm.sf((np.log(TIMES)[None, :] - mu[:, None]) / AFT_SCALE)
    pre, estimator = model['pre'], model['model']
    z = pre.transform(x)
    risk = estimator.predict(z)
    survival = None if name == 'SVM' else np.asarray([s(TIMES) for s in estimator.predict_survival_function(z)])
    return risk, survival

Step 9 — Assess performance with internal validation¶

I use five outer folds around the three-fold tuning. Each outer prediction comes from a model that did not see that patient's data. I report C-index, three-year IPCW C-index/AUC, Brier score and integrated Brier score (IBS, years 1–3), using scikit-survival metrics. For horizon-specific evaluation only, later observations are administratively censored just after three years; this preserves all earlier information and keeps IPCW evaluation within each training fold's follow-up. Training retains full follow-up.

In [9]:
def evaluate(reference, target, risk, survival):
    time, event = target['rfstime'], target['status']
    horizon_y = Surv.from_arrays(event & (time <= HORIZON), np.minimum(time, HORIZON + 1))
    horizon_risk = risk if survival is None else 1 - survival[:, -1]
    row = {'C-index': concordance_index_censored(event, time, risk)[0],
           'Uno C-index (3y)': concordance_index_ipcw(reference, horizon_y, horizon_risk, tau=HORIZON)[0],
           'AUC (3y)': cumulative_dynamic_auc(reference, horizon_y, horizon_risk, [HORIZON])[0][0],
           'Brier (3y)': np.nan, 'IBS (1-3y)': np.nan}
    if survival is not None:
        row['Brier (3y)'] = brier_score(reference, horizon_y, survival[:, -1:], [HORIZON])[1][0]
        row['IBS (1-3y)'] = integrated_brier_score(reference, horizon_y, survival, TIMES)
    return row

cv_rows, parameter_rows = [], []
oof_survival = {name: np.zeros((len(X_train), len(TIMES))) for name in probability_names}
outer = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
for fold, (tr, va) in enumerate(outer.split(X_train, y_train['status']), 1):
    for name in names:
        model, parameters = fit_model(name, X_train.iloc[tr], y_train[tr])
        risk, survival = predict_model(name, model, X_train.iloc[va])
        cv_rows.append({'Fold': fold, 'Model': name, **evaluate(y_train[tr], y_train[va], risk, survival)})
        parameter_rows.append({'Fold': fold, 'Model': name, 'Parameters': json.dumps(parameters)})
        if survival is not None:
            oof_survival[name][va] = survival
    print(f'Outer fold {fold}/5 completed')
cv_results = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows)
display(cv_results.groupby('Model')[list(cv_results.columns[2:])].agg(['mean', 'std']).round(3))
cv_results.to_csv(OUT / 'nested_cv_results.csv', index=False)
pd.DataFrame(parameter_rows).to_csv(OUT / 'nested_cv_parameters.csv', index=False)

I check calibration using four groups of out-of-fold three-year risk. The observed risks come from Kaplan–Meier estimates, so censored patients are retained. Points near the diagonal indicate better calibration. These grouped curves are descriptive; five folds do not provide a precise performance confidence interval.

In [10]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
calibration_rows = []
for name in probability_names:
    predicted = 1 - oof_survival[name][:, -1]
    groups = pd.qcut(predicted, q=4, duplicates='drop')
    points = []
    for group in groups.categories:
        ix = groups == group
        km = KaplanMeierFitter().fit(y_train['rfstime'][ix], y_train['status'][ix])
        observed = 1 - km.predict(HORIZON)
        points.append([predicted[ix].mean(), observed])
        calibration_rows.append({'Model': name, 'Patients': int(ix.sum()),
                                  'Predicted': predicted[ix].mean(), 'KM observed': observed})
    ax.plot(*np.asarray(points).T, marker='o', label=name)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], '--', color='grey')
ax.set(xlabel='Predicted three-year event risk', ylabel='Observed three-year event risk (KM)',
       title='Calibration: development out-of-fold predictions', xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1))
ax.legend()
plt.savefig(OUT / 'oof_calibration.png', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()
pd.DataFrame(calibration_rows).to_csv(OUT / 'oof_calibration.csv', index=False)

Step 10 — Decide on the final model¶

I choose the lowest mean outer-validation IBS among models that estimate absolute survival probabilities. This assesses calibration and discrimination together. SVM remains in the ranking comparison but cannot be selected as an absolute-risk calculator without an additional model. Nested validation addresses development optimism; it is not a bootstrap optimism-correction estimate. I now lock the choice, retune on all development patients, and evaluate the holdout once.

In [11]:
cv_mean = cv_results.groupby('Model').mean(numeric_only=True)
selected = cv_mean['IBS (1-3y)'].dropna().idxmin()
print('Selected probability model, before holdout evaluation:', selected)
fitted, final_parameters, predictions, test_rows = {}, {}, {}, []
for name in names:
    start = perf_counter()
    fitted[name], final_parameters[name] = fit_model(name, X_train, y_train)
    fit_seconds = perf_counter() - start
    risk, survival = predict_model(name, fitted[name], X_test)
    predictions[name] = (risk, survival)
    ci = bootstrap((y_test['status'], y_test['rfstime'], risk),
                   lambda e, t, r: concordance_index_censored(e.astype(bool), t, r)[0],
                   paired=True, vectorized=False, n_resamples=1000,
                   method='percentile', random_state=SEED).confidence_interval
    test_rows.append({'Model': name, **evaluate(y_train, y_test, risk, survival),
                      'C-index lower': ci.low, 'C-index upper': ci.high,
                      'Tuning + fit seconds': fit_seconds})
test_results = pd.DataFrame(test_rows).set_index('Model')
display(test_results.round(3))
test_results.to_csv(OUT / 'holdout_performance.csv')
display(pd.DataFrame({'Best development parameters': final_parameters}))

Step 11 — Decision curve analysis¶

I use Python dcurves with the survival outcome and three-year probabilities. The hypothetical action is closer follow-up above a risk threshold. I compare the probability models with acting on everyone or no one. The 5–60% range is illustrative, not a clinically agreed policy; SVM is omitted because its raw ranking is not a probability.

In [13]:
decision_data = df.iloc[test_id][['status', 'rfstime']].reset_index(drop=True).copy()
for name in probability_names:
    decision_data[name] = 1 - predictions[name][1][:, -1]
decision_curves = dca(data=decision_data, outcome='status', modelnames=probability_names,
                      thresholds=np.arange(0.05, 0.601, 0.01), time=HORIZON,
                      time_to_outcome_col='rfstime')
ax = decision_curves.pivot(index='threshold', columns='model', values='net_benefit').plot()
ax.set(xlabel='Three-year event-risk threshold', ylabel='Net benefit',
       title='Holdout decision curves: models, all and none', ylim=(-0.10, 0.4))
plt.savefig(OUT / 'decision_curves.png', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()
decision_curves.to_csv(OUT / 'decision_curves.csv', index=False)

Step 12 — Assess individual predictors (optional)¶

I use scikit-learn's permutation importance for the forest, measured as the drop in holdout C-index. This is a post-hoc explanation, not another selection step. Correlated predictors can share importance, and importance does not show causation.

In [14]:
importance = permutation_importance(fitted['RForest'], X_test, y_test,
                                    n_repeats=20, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=1)
importance_table = pd.DataFrame({'Mean C-index decrease': importance.importances_mean,
                                 'Repeat SD': importance.importances_std}, index=features).sort_values('Mean C-index decrease')
importance_table['Mean C-index decrease'].plot.barh(xerr=importance_table['Repeat SD'], color='#277da8')
plt.xlabel('Decrease in C-index after shuffling the predictor')
plt.title('Forest permutation importance on the holdout')
plt.savefig(OUT / 'forest_importance.png', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()
importance_table.to_csv(OUT / 'forest_importance.csv')

Additional analysis — reliability and interpretation¶

I keep the original split, tuning and selected model unchanged. These extra checks are exploratory because I have already examined the holdout. Reliability includes ranking, absolute-risk accuracy and sensitivity to the development sample. SHAP explains the fitted models; it cannot establish predictive accuracy or causality.

A. Prediction error and overfitting¶

I compare apparent training performance with nested validation and the holdout. For absolute-risk models I also compare IPCW Brier scores with a Kaplan–Meier model fitted to the development set without predictors. Positive Brier skill means improvement over this reference. Fold SD describes variation, not a confidence interval.

In [15]:
import shap
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
REL = OUT / 'reliability'
REL.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
horizon_test = Surv.from_arrays(y_test['status'] & (y_test['rfstime'] <= HORIZON),
                               np.minimum(y_test['rfstime'], HORIZON + 1))
km_null = KaplanMeierFitter().fit(y_train['rfstime'], y_train['status'])
null_survival = np.tile(km_null.predict(TIMES).to_numpy(), (len(y_test), 1))
null_ibs = integrated_brier_score(y_train, horizon_test, null_survival, TIMES)
reliability = test_results[['C-index', 'Brier (3y)', 'IBS (1-3y)']].copy()
for name in names:
    train_risk, _ = predict_model(name, fitted[name], X_train)
    reliability.loc[name, 'Apparent training C'] = concordance_index_censored(
        y_train['status'], y_train['rfstime'], train_risk)[0]
    reliability.loc[name, 'Nested CV C mean'] = cv_mean.loc[name, 'C-index']
    reliability.loc[name, 'Nested CV C SD'] = cv_results.query('Model == @name')['C-index'].std()
reliability['Training minus CV C'] = reliability['Apparent training C'] - reliability['Nested CV C mean']
reliability['IBS skill vs KM'] = 1 - reliability['IBS (1-3y)'] / null_ibs
reliability.to_csv(REL / 'reliability_comparison.csv')
display(reliability.round(3))
print(f'No-predictor Kaplan–Meier holdout IBS: {null_ibs:.3f}')
for name in probability_names:
    loss = brier_score(y_train, horizon_test, predictions[name][1], TIMES)[1]
    plt.plot(TIMES / 365.25, loss, label=name)
plt.plot(TIMES / 365.25, brier_score(y_train, horizon_test, null_survival, TIMES)[1],
         '--', color='grey', label='Development KM')
plt.xlabel('Years'); plt.ylabel('IPCW Brier score (lower is better)')
plt.title('Holdout prediction error over time'); plt.legend()
plt.savefig(REL / 'brier_over_time.png', bbox_inches='tight'); plt.show()

B. Are the differences from Cox convincing?¶

I use SciPy bootstrap to resample the same holdout patient indices for every model, keeping their outcomes and predictions together. The 2,000 paired resamples give percentile 95% intervals for differences from Cox. Positive C-index differences and negative IBS differences favour ML. The censoring distribution stays estimated from development data. These exploratory intervals condition on the fitted models and are not adjusted for multiple comparisons; an interval crossing zero does not establish equivalence.

In [16]:
comparison_keys = [(name, 'C-index') for name in names if name != 'Cox'] + [
    (name, 'IBS (1-3y)') for name in probability_names if name != 'Cox']

def paired_differences(indices):
    ix = indices.astype(int)
    c = {name: concordance_index_censored(y_test['status'][ix], y_test['rfstime'][ix],
                                          predictions[name][0][ix])[0] for name in names}
    ibs = {name: integrated_brier_score(y_train, horizon_test[ix], predictions[name][1][ix], TIMES)
           for name in probability_names}
    return np.array([(c[name] - c['Cox']) if metric == 'C-index' else (ibs[name] - ibs['Cox'])
                     for name, metric in comparison_keys])

paired_boot = bootstrap((np.arange(len(y_test)),), paired_differences, vectorized=False,
                         n_resamples=2000, method='percentile', random_state=SEED)
paired_results = pd.DataFrame(comparison_keys, columns=['Model', 'Metric'])
paired_results['Difference vs Cox'] = paired_differences(np.arange(len(y_test)))
paired_results['95% lower'] = paired_boot.confidence_interval.low
paired_results['95% upper'] = paired_boot.confidence_interval.high
paired_results.to_csv(REL / 'paired_differences_vs_cox.csv', index=False)
np.save(REL / 'paired_bootstrap_differences.npy', paired_boot.bootstrap_distribution)
display(paired_results.round(4))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
for ax, metric in zip(axes, ['C-index', 'IBS (1-3y)']):
    rows = paired_results.query('Metric == @metric')
    ax.errorbar(rows['Difference vs Cox'], np.arange(len(rows)),
                xerr=np.vstack([rows['Difference vs Cox'] - rows['95% lower'],
                                rows['95% upper'] - rows['Difference vs Cox']]), fmt='o', capsize=4)
    ax.axvline(0, color='grey', linestyle='--')
    ax.set(yticks=np.arange(len(rows)), yticklabels=rows.Model,
           xlabel=f'{metric}: model minus Cox', title='Higher favours ML' if metric == 'C-index' else 'Lower favours ML')
fig.suptitle('Paired holdout differences: 95% bootstrap intervals')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(REL / 'paired_differences.png', bbox_inches='tight'); plt.show()

C. Calibration with uncertainty¶

I split each probability model's holdout risks into quartiles. Observed three-year risk is one minus Kaplan–Meier survival; bars use its Greenwood log-log 95% interval. Groups contain about 34 patients, so wide bars are expected. These are grouped calibration estimates, not individual prediction intervals. SVM has no absolute-risk output, so calibration and Brier skill cannot be assessed for it.

In [17]:
cal_rows = []
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, name in zip(axes, probability_names):
    probability = 1 - predictions[name][1][:, -1]
    groups = pd.qcut(probability, 4, duplicates='drop')
    for group in groups.categories:
        ix = groups == group
        km = KaplanMeierFitter().fit(y_test['rfstime'][ix], y_test['status'][ix])
        observed = 1 - km.predict(HORIZON)
        ci = km.confidence_interval_survival_function_.loc[:HORIZON].iloc[-1]
        lower, upper = 1 - ci.iloc[1], 1 - ci.iloc[0]
        cal_rows.append({'Model': name, 'Patients': int(ix.sum()),
                         'Events by 3y': int((y_test['status'][ix] & (y_test['rfstime'][ix] <= HORIZON)).sum()),
                         'At risk at 3y': int((y_test['rfstime'][ix] >= HORIZON).sum()),
                         'Predicted': probability[ix].mean(), 'KM observed': observed,
                         '95% lower': lower, '95% upper': upper})
        ax.errorbar(probability[ix].mean(), observed,
                    yerr=[[observed - lower], [upper - observed]], fmt='o', capsize=3)
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], '--', color='grey')
    ax.set(title=name, xlabel='Predicted event risk', xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1))
axes[0].set_ylabel('Observed event risk (KM, 95% CI)')
fig.suptitle('Three-year holdout calibration')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(REL / 'holdout_calibration_intervals.png', bbox_inches='tight'); plt.show()
pd.DataFrame(cal_rows).to_csv(REL / 'holdout_calibration_intervals.csv', index=False)

D. Sensitivity to the development sample¶

I refit each model on 50 bootstrap samples of development patients, including preprocessing. Hyperparameters and algorithm seeds stay fixed; the holdout is unchanged. Spearman correlation with the original risk ranking measures ranking stability. For probability models, I also measure each patient's 2.5–97.5 percentile risk range. These exploratory ranges show training-sample sensitivity, conditional on the selected settings. They exclude tuning uncertainty and do not guarantee coverage or accuracy. A stable model can still be biased. I also record the SVM optimizer's success flag for every refit, retaining flagged refits in the stability summaries and reporting their number.

In [18]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
boot_risks = {name: np.empty((50, len(X_test))) for name in names}
boot_probabilities = {name: np.empty((50, len(X_test))) for name in probability_names}
stability_rows, optimizer_rows = [], []
for b in range(50):
    ix = rng.integers(len(X_train), size=len(X_train))
    for name in names:
        if name == 'XGBoost':
            pre = clone(fitted[name][0])
            train = xgb.DMatrix(pre.fit_transform(X_train.iloc[ix]), label_lower_bound=y_train['rfstime'][ix],
                                label_upper_bound=np.where(y_train['status'][ix], y_train['rfstime'][ix], np.inf))
            model = (pre, xgb.train(aft_params | final_parameters[name], train, num_boost_round=150))
        else:
            model = clone(fitted[name]).fit(X_train.iloc[ix], y_train[ix])
        if name == 'SVM':
            status = model['model'].optimizer_result_
            optimizer_rows.append({'Refit': b + 1, 'Converged': bool(status.success),
                                    'Optimizer message': str(status.message)})
        risk, survival = predict_model(name, model, X_test)
        boot_risks[name][b] = risk
        stability_rows.append({'Refit': b + 1, 'Model': name,
                               'Risk rank correlation': spearmanr(predictions[name][0], risk).statistic})
        if survival is not None:
            boot_probabilities[name][b] = 1 - survival[:, -1]
    if (b + 1) % 10 == 0:
        print(f'Bootstrap refits {b + 1}/50 completed')
stability_draws = pd.DataFrame(stability_rows)
optimizer_checks = pd.DataFrame(optimizer_rows)
optimizer_checks.to_csv(REL / 'svm_optimizer_checks.csv', index=False)
print(f'SVM optimizer reported success in {optimizer_checks.Converged.sum()}/50 refits.')
stability_summary = stability_draws.groupby('Model')['Risk rank correlation'].agg(['median', 'min'])
patient_ranges = []
for name in probability_names:
    lower, upper = np.quantile(boot_probabilities[name], [0.025, 0.975], axis=0)
    stability_summary.loc[name, 'Median probability range width'] = np.median(upper - lower)
    patient_ranges.extend({'pid': int(pid), 'Model': name, '2.5% risk': lo, '97.5% risk': hi,
                           'Range width': hi - lo} for pid, lo, hi in zip(df.pid.iloc[test_id], lower, upper))
display(stability_summary.round(3))
stability_draws.to_csv(REL / 'training_bootstrap_rank_stability.csv', index=False)
stability_summary.to_csv(REL / 'training_bootstrap_summary.csv')
pd.DataFrame(patient_ranges).to_csv(REL / 'patient_probability_ranges.csv', index=False)
np.savez_compressed(REL / 'training_bootstrap_predictions.npz', pid=df.pid.iloc[test_id].to_numpy(),
                     **{f'{name}_risk': a for name, a in boot_risks.items()},
                     **{f'{name}_probability': a for name, a in boot_probabilities.items()})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
stability_draws.boxplot(column='Risk rank correlation', by='Model', ax=axes[0])
pd.DataFrame(patient_ranges).boxplot(column='Range width', by='Model', ax=axes[1])
axes[0].set(title='Ranking stability: 50 development refits', ylabel='Spearman correlation with original ranking')
axes[1].set(title='Sensitivity of three-year risk', ylabel='Patient probability range width')

E. SHAP explanations on the original eight predictors¶

I use the package's PermutationExplainer for all models, so preprocessing and grade encoding remain inside the prediction function. The same 30 randomly selected development patients provide the background; I explain 50 randomly selected holdout patients, using five forward/reverse permutation cycles per patient. These are approximate SHAP estimates.

Cox, forest and XGBoost explain three-year event probability: positive values raise risk relative to the background. SVM explains its ranking score on a separate scale. Independent masking can create unusual combinations of correlated features, such as ER and progesterone receptor. Attributions depend on this background and are not causal effects. No new features or models are selected from these plots.

In [19]:
background = X_train.sample(n=30, random_state=SEED)
explain_x = X_test.sample(n=50, random_state=SEED)
shap_values, shap_importance, shap_checks = {}, {}, []

def explanation_output(values, name):
    risk, survival = predict_model(name, fitted[name], pd.DataFrame(values, columns=features))
    return risk if name == 'SVM' else 1 - survival[:, -1]

for name in names:
    explainer = shap.PermutationExplainer(lambda values, name=name: explanation_output(values, name),
                                         background, seed=SEED)
    explanation = explainer(explain_x, max_evals=5 * (2 * len(features) + 1), silent=True)
    shap_values[name] = explanation
    output = explanation_output(explain_x.to_numpy(), name)
    error = np.max(np.abs(explanation.base_values + explanation.values.sum(axis=1) - output))
    assert error < 1e-5, f'{name}: SHAP additivity check failed'
    shap_checks.append({'Model': name, 'Max reconstruction error': error})
    shap_importance[name] = np.abs(explanation.values).mean(axis=0)
    table = pd.DataFrame(explanation.values, columns=features)
    table.insert(0, 'pid', df.loc[explain_x.index, 'pid'].to_numpy())
    table['Background output'] = explanation.base_values
    table['Model output'] = output
    table.to_csv(REL / f'shap_values_{name}.csv', index=False)
    shap.plots.beeswarm(explanation, max_display=8, show=False)
    plt.xlabel('SHAP value: SVM ranking score' if name == 'SVM' else 'SHAP value: three-year event probability')
    plt.title(f'{name}: SHAP on 50 holdout patients')
    plt.savefig(REL / f'shap_beeswarm_{name}.png', bbox_inches='tight'); plt.show()
    print(f'{name}: explanations completed; maximum reconstruction error {error:.2g}')
shap_importance = pd.DataFrame(shap_importance, index=features)
shap_importance.to_csv(REL / 'shap_mean_absolute.csv')
pd.DataFrame(shap_checks).to_csv(REL / 'shap_additivity_checks.csv', index=False)
joblib.dump(shap_values, REL / 'shap_explanations.joblib', compress=3)
df.loc[background.index, ['pid'] + features].to_csv(REL / 'shap_background.csv', index=False)
df.loc[explain_x.index, ['pid'] + features].to_csv(REL / 'shap_explained_patients.csv', index=False)

F. What can I conclude about reliability?¶

I combine uncertainty, calibration, stability and interpretation rather than use a single score. The original XGBoost choice stays locked to the prespecified nested-CV IBS rule. Additional holdout analyses are descriptive and cannot replace external validation. The summary below is generated from the results above.

In [21]:
no_clear_difference = ((paired_results['95% lower'] <= 0) & (paired_results['95% upper'] >= 0)).all()
most_stable = stability_summary['median'].idxmax()
summary_text = (
    f"**Reliability conclusion:** {'All paired ML-versus-Cox 95% intervals include zero; there is no convincing overall winner in this holdout.' if no_clear_difference else 'Some paired intervals exclude zero; assess their metric and direction in the comparison table before claiming an advantage.'} "
    "This is not evidence that the models are equivalent.\n\n"
    f"- **Random forest:** holdout C-index {test_results.loc['RForest', 'C-index']:.3f}; "
    f"IBS {test_results.loc['RForest', 'IBS (1-3y)']:.3f}.\n"
    f"- **Cox:** holdout C-index {test_results.loc['Cox', 'C-index']:.3f}; "
    f"IBS {test_results.loc['Cox', 'IBS (1-3y)']:.3f}.\n"
    f"- **XGBoost:** selected using nested CV; holdout C-index {test_results.loc['XGBoost', 'C-index']:.3f}; "
    f"IBS {test_results.loc['XGBoost', 'IBS (1-3y)']:.3f}.\n"
    f"- **SVM:** holdout C-index {test_results.loc['SVM', 'C-index']:.3f}; absolute-risk reliability remains unassessed.\n\n"
    f"**{most_stable}** has the highest median ranking correlation across the 50 training refits "
    f"({stability_summary.loc[most_stable, 'median']:.3f}); stability alone does not establish accuracy. "
    "SHAP identifies the largest average contributors in the explained holdout sample: "
    + '; '.join(f"{name}: {shap_importance[name].idxmax()}" for name in names)
    + ". These are model explanations, not independent evidence of biomarker validity.\n\n"
    f"The SVM optimizer reported success in **{optimizer_checks.Converged.sum()}/50** refits. "
    "Flagged precision-loss refits are retained in the stability summary; their presence limits "
    "a claim of numerical reliability.\n\n"
    f"For absolute-risk stability, median patient risk-range widths were "
    f"**{stability_summary.loc['Cox', 'Median probability range width']:.3f} for Cox**, "
    f"**{stability_summary.loc['RForest', 'Median probability range width']:.3f} for forest** and "
    f"**{stability_summary.loc['XGBoost', 'Median probability range width']:.3f} for XGBoost**. "
    "These are probability-unit ranges across development refits. Cox therefore has narrower "
    "ranges than the forest in this experiment, alongside a smaller training-to-validation gap.\n\n"
    "The 138-patient holdout and wide calibration intervals limit certainty. I would retain Cox "
    "as a strong, simple reference and describe the ML models as alternatives requiring larger external validation, "
    "rather than claim that SHAP establishes a more reliable model."
)
(REL / 'reliability_summary.md').write_text(summary_text)
display(Markdown(summary_text))

Reliability conclusion: All paired ML-versus-Cox 95% intervals include zero; there is no convincing overall winner in this holdout. This is not evidence that the models are equivalent.

  • Random forest: holdout C-index 0.716; IBS 0.150.
  • Cox: holdout C-index 0.700; IBS 0.151.
  • XGBoost: selected using nested CV; holdout C-index 0.705; IBS 0.157.
  • SVM: holdout C-index 0.695; absolute-risk reliability remains unassessed.

SVM has the highest median ranking correlation across the 50 training refits (0.960); stability alone does not establish accuracy. SHAP identifies the largest average contributors in the explained holdout sample: Cox: pgr; RForest: nodes; XGBoost: nodes; SVM: pgr. These are model explanations, not independent evidence of biomarker validity.

The SVM optimizer reported success in 48/50 refits. Flagged precision-loss refits are retained in the stability summary; their presence limits a claim of numerical reliability.

For absolute-risk stability, median patient risk-range widths were 0.196 for Cox, 0.275 for forest and 0.200 for XGBoost. These are probability-unit ranges across development refits. Cox therefore has narrower ranges than the forest in this experiment, alongside a smaller training-to-validation gap.

The 138-patient holdout and wide calibration intervals limit certainty. I would retain Cox as a strong, simple reference and describe the ML models as alternatives requiring larger external validation, rather than claim that SHAP establishes a more reliable model.

Step 13 — Write up and make the model reusable¶

I report the cohort, outcome, predictor coding, missingness, tuning, internal validation and holdout results, following the supplied workflow and TRIPOD. I save all fitted models with their preprocessing and show one held-out example. There is no external validation. The source data were already selected for completeness, and the historical, node-positive trial population limits generalisation. The models estimate prognosis, not the causal benefit of changing hormonal therapy.

In [22]:

Reusing the saved models¶

The saved bundle contains standard package estimators, not custom estimator classes. Use the same eight columns in features. Cox/forest/SVM pipelines accept raw predictors; XGBoost stores its fitted preprocessor and native booster together. Only load a joblib file from a trusted source. These are development-set fits (548 patients), whose holdout performance is reported above, not full-cohort refits.
